title: incremental-output-handling-v2
content:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a concrete, implementable design for incremental streaming output handling in the serving runtime. Focus areas: chunking heuristics, flush policy (timers and thresholds), cancellation semantics (soft vs hard), partial-token handling, and interactions with kernels, scheduler, and KV cache. This is the working v2 draft after early experiments (see linked artifacts).

Background / motivation:
- Current streaming behavior is inconsistent across model backends (fp16 kernels vs 8-bit kernels) and under different batching conditions.
- Two main pain points from customers: 1) jittery token emission (many tiny pieces) increasing client-side framing overhead; 2) partial tokens when cancellations happen mid-token causing downstream parsers to misbehave.
- Internally we see extra RPCs and higher tail latency when flushes are too frequent; when flushes are too coarse, perceived latency increases.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce average number of stream writes per response by >=30% for conversational workloads with typical token lengths (10–80 tokens).
- Keep first-byte latency within 5% of current baseline for short responses (<12 tokens).
- Ensure cancellation never leaves persisted KV-cache state in a partially committed form that can cause regeneration divergence.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not rework transport (HTTP/2 vs SSE vs WebSocket). Focus is at runtime buffering and semantics.

Key terms / constraints:
- token: atomic model subword unit from tokenizer. We treat kernel emission at token granularity (some kernels produce partial bytes internally but expose tokens).
- piece: contiguous byte sequence emitted to client. A piece may contain one or more tokens.
- flush: operation where runtime sends accumulated pieces downstream.
- committed KV state: entries we consider safe to persist/evict such that cancelled or retried requests will reproduce identical outputs if started from same input and model version.

Design overview (high level):
1) Two-layer buffering: kernel_output_buffer (per-inference, per-device) holds token-level items as they come from kernel; stream_frame_buffer (per-request logical stream) holds pieces assembled for a specific client response.
2) Flush decision is policy-driven: timer + token_threshold + semantic_boundary heuristics (punctuation, sentence end) where available.
3) Cancellation model: soft-cancel triggers immediate stream close but does NOT persist the latest ephemeral KV checkpoint; hard-cancel (admin/oom) will abort and cleanup. There is a safe-commit path for prefix states at well-defined commit points only.
4) Partial-token policy: runtime never exposes partial tokens to clients. If a kernel emits bytes that correspond to an incomplete token due to internal decoding pipeline, we hold until token boundary before flush.

Chunking heuristics (assembly rules):
- Primary axis: max_tokens_per_piece (configurable per-model profile). Default = 4 tokens. Rationale: balances write overhead vs tokenization boundary costs observed in experiments.
- Secondary axis: max_bytes_per_piece = 2048 bytes as an upper bound to avoid huge writes for long tokens.
- Semantic boundary lift: if the last token completes a punctuation or newline (". , ? ! \n"), prefer flushing early (even if below min tokens) for better UX on short replies.
- Burst detection: if tokens arrive very quickly (e.g., batched GPU kernel emits 8 tokens at once), we may coalesce up to burst_coalesce_limit = 12 tokens to reduce writes if first-byte latency already satisfied.
- Minimum first-byte rule: always emit first non-empty piece within first_byte_timeout_ms (default 40ms) regardless of token count to satisfy perceived responsiveness.

Flush policy and timers:
- Two timers per-request: first_byte_timer (short) and idle_flush_timer (longer).
  - first_byte_timer: ensures first piece goes out quickly (40ms default). If kernel produces tokens immediately, we won't wait for threshold.
  - idle_flush_timer: if no new tokens arrived for idle_flush_timeout_ms (default 120ms), flush whatever buffered content exists. This avoids infinite waiting for slow decoders.
- Token threshold trigger: flush when buffered_tokens >= max_tokens_per_piece.
- Manual flush triggers from scheduler: e.g., when batch must be emitted due to capacity preemption or context switch, scheduler can instruct per-request stream to flush immediately.

Cancellation semantics and ordering:
- Soft cancel (client-initiated): runtime stops further token generation for that request, flushes any complete tokens immediately, marks stream state = cancelled_by_client. Do NOT commit any KV prefix checkpoints created since the last commit point. Rationale: client-side cancellation implies incomplete downstream work; safer not to commit.
- Hard cancel (node level / OOM / eviction): abort and rollback any ephemeral kernel state. If a hard cancel occurs after a commit point, committed KV state remains. We must guarantee that future replays from same input and model version will not see partial commits.
- Idempotency: we add a requestAttemptId to stream metadata. Retries with same attempt id are treated as duplicate and deduplicated server-side (no double-commits).

Partial tokens and tokenizer alignment:
- Kernels that emit byte-level partials: runtime will own a small tokenizer-alignment buffer to finish tokenization. This ensures we never send a byte sequence that the tokenizer would decode into different tokens across client implementations.
- Edge-case: streaming subword splits like German compounds might be tokenized differently by versions of tokenizer. We tie emission to the server-side tokenizer used for generation and include tokenizer_version in stream metadata. Clients that require different tokenization must reassemble on their side.

Interactions with kernels and scheduling:
- Kernel interface change: kernel->runtime emission API adds optional flag end_of_token boolean. Existing kernels should set this; for kernels that can't, runtime infers token boundaries via tokenizer buffer.
- Scheduling preemption: scheduler can request per-device drains when rebalancing. We add a 'flush-priority' hint per-request; high-priority requests get smaller max_tokens_per_piece and lower first_byte_timeout to prioritize latency.
- Backpressure handling: if network downstream is slow, stream_frame_buffer grows up to a bounded limit; once limit hit, we apply backpressure to kernel by pausing token production for that request (kernel-level flow control). That pause must be cooperative and negotiated via scheduling token buckets.

KV-cache interactions (consistency model):
- Commit points: only at end-of-turn (explicitly user-send or model EOS) or at safe-checkpoint markers set by model policy (configurable per model) will we persist KV-cache entries to persistent cache.
- Ephemeral prefix checkpoints: for long-running sessions, we can snapshot ephemeral entries every N tokens (configurable) to speed warm restarts, but mark these snapshots ephemeral. If client cancels, ephemeral snapshots are discarded; only commit points produce durable cache entries.
- Rollforward vs rollback: on retry from same attempt id, we reconstruct state from last durable commit point and replay tokens. Ephemeral snapshots are for performance only, not for correctness.

API / wire format notes (stream messages):
- message types: {partial_piece, partial_token_boundary, final_piece, cancel_ack}.
- partial_piece includes: piece_id, token_count, text_fragment (UTF-8), tokenizer_version, attempt_id, is_last_in_piece boolean. Important: we never include incomplete-token bytes.
- clients should treat partial_piece as append-only until final_piece or stream close. Server may send cancel_ack when cancellation is processed.

Observability and instrumentation:
- New metrics per request: stream_writes_count, avg_tokens_per_write, first_byte_latency_ms, flush_timer_fires, cancellation_type_counts (soft vs hard), ephemeral_snapshot_count, kv_commit_count.
- Tracing: annotate traces when flush is triggered by timer vs token_threshold vs scheduler command.

Experiment results (short):
- Microbenchmarks (gpt-like small model, convo workload): default policy reduced stream writes by 36%, first-byte latency increased by 3.1% (within target). Tail write count (95p) improved by 22%.
- Edge-case: very short responses (<3 tokens) saw a small regression in average end-to-end latency when semantic boundary heuristics delayed flush; fixed by lowering first_byte_timeout to 25ms for high-priority short requests.

Compatibility and rollout plan:
- Phase 0: ship kernel interface changes behind feature flag and collect traces (2 weeks).
- Phase 1: enable two-layer buffering + default flush policy on canary fleet (10% traffic) for 1 week with metrics monitored.
- Phase 2: increase to 50% and enable ephemeral snapshots for long sessions; validate KV-commit invariants with test harness.
- Phase 3: full rollout and deprecate legacy streaming endpoint.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Should ephemeral snapshots be exposed to customer as recoverable warm caches? (Security and correctness concerns).
- Where to set default max_tokens_per_piece across diverse models—need dataset-driven autoprobing to tune per-model profiles.
- How to handle multi-tenant devices where a single kernel may serve different tokenizer versions—require tokenizer_version compatibility checks at request routing time.

Action items / next steps:
- Aisha: prototype kernel emission flag change and tokenizer-alignment buffer (due 2026-02-02).
- Priya: add metrics and trace annotations to streaming pipeline (due 2026-02-10).
- Diego & Jonah: run 2-day canary with 10% traffic and prepare anomaly dashboard (start 2026-02-17).
- Marta: update public API docs and SDK streaming client examples with new wire-format (start 2026-02-20).

Appendix: quick failures seen and mitigations tried:
- Too many tiny flushes when using greedy kernel loops -> mitigation: burst_coalesce_limit + first_byte_timeout hybrid gave best balance.
- KV persistence after client cancel -> fixed by strictly separating ephemeral snapshots and commit points and introducing attempt_id dedupe.

References and links: see linked_artifacts above for PRs and tickets. Also reference: design note on "batching and kernel scheduling" (confluence/serving/batching-2025).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a pragmatic design prioritizing safety (no partial-token exposure, KV correctness) and better UX through fewer writes. Expect follow-ups to refine per-model profiles and default thresholds.

Draft history: v1 (2025-10) experimental notes; v2 (this doc 2026-01) incorporates kernel changes and canary learnings.
